commissions.title: Evaluate and improve an individual questionnaire item
commissions.specification_text:
Create a focused Practice experience for university researchers in which learners independently evaluate an individual questionnaire item, explain a consequential design weakness, propose a justified improvement and refine their response after explanatory feedback. The educational job is to establish the connection between questionnaire design, methodological consequences and justified improvement through one complete, tightly bounded practice cycle.

RESEARCH CONTEXT AND QUESTIONNAIRE EVIDENCE
Use a realistic but explicitly constructed example concerning university students' experiences of academic support. The researcher wishes to investigate currently enrolled students' satisfaction with the availability of academic support. For this example, academic support means opportunities to obtain help with course-related learning from university teaching and support staff.

Present the following draft questionnaire item: 'How satisfied are you with the availability and quality of academic support at your university?' Response options: Very dissatisfied; Dissatisfied; Neither satisfied nor dissatisfied; Satisfied; Very satisfied.

Make clear that this questionnaire item has been constructed for the learning experience and is not taken from an actual research instrument. The example is first-pass unfamiliar evidence, but its subject matter and response format should be readily recognisable. Assume general familiarity with questionnaires, research objectives and the purpose of collecting respondent data. Do not assume specialist knowledge of questionnaire methodology or require learners to study an introductory explanation before attempting the task.

INDEPENDENT PRACTICE
Provide three explicit procedural prompts that support the learner's evaluative reasoning without revealing the diagnosis:
1. Identify one consequential weakness in the questionnaire item in relation to the research objective.
2. Explain how this weakness could affect respondents' answers or the usefulness of the resulting data.
3. Propose an improved questionnaire item and briefly justify your revision.

The expected response is approximately three or four short sentences together with the revised item. Learners may retain or change the response options as appropriate to their proposed improvement. Concentrate on one consequential weakness rather than requiring exhaustive evaluation. Do not provide diagnostic answer options, a worked example or substantive methodological hints before the independent attempt.

EXPLANATORY FEEDBACK
After the learner has attempted the evaluation, provide concise explanatory feedback grounded in the actual questionnaire item. Explain that the item combines availability and quality, which respondents may evaluate differently. A student might be satisfied with the quality of support when it is available but dissatisfied with how difficult it is to access. A single satisfaction response cannot distinguish these experiences, making the resulting evidence difficult to interpret in relation to the stated research objective.

Illustrate a defensible revision: 'How satisfied are you with the availability of academic support at your university?' Retain the five-point satisfaction scale. Explain that narrowing the question to availability improves alignment with the intended construct and makes the response more interpretable.

Acknowledge that separating availability and quality into two questions would also be defensible if the research objective included both constructs, although this would increase questionnaire length. Recognise that learners may identify another consequential issue, such as whether students without sufficient experience of academic support can answer meaningfully. Explain that the appropriateness of a non-applicable response option or eligibility instruction depends on the intended respondent population and the meaning of availability within the research design.

Keep feedback focused on the relationship between design decisions and methodological consequences. Do not imply that the illustrative revision is the only acceptable answer or that it has been empirically validated.

IMPROVEMENT
Invite learners to revisit their existing response and improve one aspect of their evaluation, methodological explanation, proposed revision or justification. If their original response is already defensible, encourage them to make the rationale more precise or acknowledge a relevant limitation. The improvement should require a small, meaningful edit rather than a separate reflective response.

WORKLOAD AND SCAFFOLDING
The authoritative allocation is five minutes of complete learner effort. Internally design for approximately one minute of contextual reading, activation of familiar knowledge and first-pass inspection; two minutes of independent reasoning and response construction; one minute of explanatory feedback engagement; and one minute of refinement. Keep the scenario, questionnaire item, task instructions and feedback sufficiently concise to make this complete cycle achievable. The explicit prompts provide procedural scaffolding without supplying the diagnosis. Do not introduce separate introductory teaching, knowledge testing, extended reflection or additional practice items. No real survey data, specialist software, external research or tutor participation is required. Keep internal timing allocations out of learner-facing prose and do not frame completion speed as a performance criterion.

LEARNER EVIDENCE AND JOURNAL CONTRACT
Declare elicitation_id E1 for the substantive learner-authored written evaluation, methodological explanation, revised questionnaire item and justification. The elicitation must allow the learner to improve the same response following feedback. Retain this as one coherent learner-authored artefact available through the journey-level Learning Journal as comm_1.E1. Do not require additional journal writing or transcription. Do not assume that a separate pre-feedback response is retained.

SUCCESS EXPECTATIONS
A defensible performance identifies a consequential weakness in relation to the research objective, explains a plausible methodological consequence and proposes an improvement that addresses the weakness without unnecessarily changing the intended construct. The learner has a meaningful opportunity to strengthen the response after engaging with feedback. Judge the quality of the reasoning rather than conformity to the illustrative wording.

commissions.title: Evaluate and improve several questionnaire items
commissions.specification_text:
Create a Practice experience for university researchers that extends questionnaire item evaluation across three short items associated with a shared research objective. The educational job is to develop discrimination between different questionnaire design weaknesses, more precise explanations of their methodological consequences and greater independence in selecting and justifying appropriate improvements. Preserve the complete cycle of independent evaluation, explanatory feedback and targeted improvement.

RESEARCH CONTEXT AND QUESTIONNAIRE EVIDENCE
Use a realistic but explicitly constructed questionnaire scenario concerning university students' use of campus study spaces. The research objective is to understand how frequently students use campus study spaces, how satisfied they are with the suitability of those spaces for their study needs, and what barriers may limit their use. The intended respondents are currently enrolled students, including those who rarely or never use campus study spaces. For this example, campus study spaces include libraries, designated study rooms and shared areas provided by the university for independent or collaborative study.

Present three draft questionnaire items with their complete response options.

Item 1: 'How often do you use the university's study spaces?' Response options: Never; Occasionally; Regularly; Frequently.

Item 2: 'How satisfied are you with the excellent study spaces provided by the university?' Response options: Very dissatisfied; Dissatisfied; Neither satisfied nor dissatisfied; Satisfied; Very satisfied.

Item 3: 'What is the main reason you do not use campus study spaces more often?' Select one response: Lack of available seats; Noise; Inconvenient location.

Make clear that these items have been constructed for learning purposes and are not taken from an actual university survey. Preserve a manageable variety of consequential weaknesses rather than making every item defective in numerous ways. The items are new first-pass unfamiliar evidence, but their subject matter and response formats remain comparable in familiarity to those used in the preceding experience. Assume general familiarity with questionnaires, research objectives and common response formats. The evaluative relationship between identifying a weakness, explaining its consequences and proposing a justified improvement has been exercised earlier in the journey. Reactivate this relationship through the task brief rather than repeat introductory teaching. Supply sufficient context for learners who access this experience independently.

INDEPENDENT PRACTICE
Provide one overarching task instruction asking learners to evaluate the three draft questionnaire items against the stated research objective and intended respondent population, explain the methodological consequences of consequential weaknesses and propose justified improvements.

For each item, expect a concise diagnosis, an explanation of its likely effects on respondents or data interpretation, a revised question or response format and a justification. Encourage learners to consider whether their proposed improvements preserve the intended construct and whether particular revisions introduce new limitations. Permit compact item-by-item responses or an equivalent structured written evaluation.

Do not provide item-specific diagnostic prompts, identify relevant design principles in advance or reveal worked revisions before the learner completes the independent attempt across the set. The learner should determine which features warrant attention and which improvements are appropriate. Exhaustive identification of every possible weakness is not required.

EXPLANATORY FEEDBACK
Provide concise, reasoned feedback on the actual questionnaire items after the independent attempt. Differentiate the methodological consequences of the weaknesses rather than simply label each item with a questionnaire design rule.

For Item 1, explain that the absence of a defined reference period and the use of subjective, potentially overlapping frequency descriptions make responses difficult to compare. Students may interpret 'regularly' and 'frequently' differently or base their answers on different periods of their university experience. Illustrate a revision such as: 'On how many days in the past four weeks have you used campus study spaces?' Response options: 0 days; 1–3 days; 4–7 days; 8–14 days; 15–28 days. Explain how a defined reference period, a specified unit of measurement and non-overlapping categories improve interpretability. Discuss the trade-off between requesting an exact number of days and offering categories: exact counts may support more flexible analysis, while categories may reduce recall and response demands. The suitability of the chosen reference period depends on whether the researcher wants to measure recent, typical or longer-term use.

For Item 2, explain how the positively evaluative word 'excellent' may encourage favourable responses or communicate the researcher's preferred judgement. Explain that the original item also leaves the basis of satisfaction relatively broad. Illustrate neutral wording aligned with the research objective, such as: 'How satisfied are you with the suitability of campus study spaces for your study needs?' Retain the balanced five-point satisfaction scale and consider a separate option such as 'Not applicable — I have not used these spaces' where appropriate. Explain that an overall satisfaction measure may be sufficient for a broad research objective, while separate questions about particular features could provide more actionable evidence at the cost of additional respondent effort. A non-applicable response should not be treated as the neutral midpoint of the satisfaction scale.

For Item 3, explain that the question assumes respondents want or need to use campus study spaces more often and that one of the listed barriers applies to them. The restricted response options may force respondents to select an inaccurate answer or prevent meaningful participation by students who experience no barriers. Illustrate a revision such as: 'Which, if any, of the following factors limit your use of campus study spaces?' Allow multiple selections from a concise, plausible set including lack of available seats, noise, inconvenient location, unsuitable opening hours, accessibility difficulties, other reasons and no factors limiting use. Specify that the no-factors option should not be selected alongside substantive barriers. Explain that multiple selection supports identification of coexisting barriers, whereas a single principal-barrier question may be appropriate if the researcher needs to prioritise one main obstacle. Recognise that some students may prefer studying elsewhere without experiencing a barrier; the treatment of this distinction should reflect the research objective.

Across the feedback, connect design decisions to respondent interpretation, response behaviour and the usefulness of the resulting evidence. Distinguish consequential methodological problems from matters of stylistic preference. Recognise credible alternative revisions and explain why their appropriateness depends on the intended research purpose. Do not imply that all questionnaire items require the same response format or that the illustrative revisions are uniquely correct.

IMPROVEMENT
Invite learners to revisit their existing evaluations and identify the aspect that would most benefit from refinement. This could involve clarifying a reference period, improving response categories, addressing an overlooked assumption, strengthening an explanation or reconsidering a design trade-off. Require a targeted improvement rather than comprehensive rewriting of all three items. Where the original decisions are already defensible, encourage greater precision in their methodological rationale or acknowledgement of a relevant limitation. Integrate the improvement into the existing response rather than introduce a separate reflective task.

WORKLOAD AND SCAFFOLDING
The authoritative allocation is fifteen minutes of complete learner effort. Internally design for approximately two minutes of contextual reading, first-pass evidence inspection and activation of familiar evaluative principles; eight minutes of independent reasoning, revision and response construction; three minutes of explanatory feedback engagement; and two minutes of targeted refinement. Keep the scenario, questionnaire items and feedback concise enough to protect this distribution of learner effort. Increase challenge through the variety of design weaknesses and the need to select appropriate improvements, not through unfamiliar disciplinary knowledge or extensive writing. Use a shared overarching instruction rather than repeated item-specific procedural scaffolding. No real survey data, specialist software, external research or tutor participation is required. Keep internal timing allocations out of learner-facing prose and do not frame completion speed as a performance criterion.

LEARNER EVIDENCE AND JOURNAL CONTRACT
Declare elicitation_id E2 for the learner's substantive written evaluations of the three questionnaire items, including methodological explanations, proposed revisions and justifications. Retain the complete performance as one coherent learner-authored artefact. The elicitation must allow the learner to improve the same response following feedback. Make its current content available through the journey-level Learning Journal as comm_2.E2. Do not require additional journal writing, reproduction of earlier work or comparison with earlier responses. Do not assume that a separate pre-feedback response is retained.

SUCCESS EXPECTATIONS
A defensible performance distinguishes consequential weaknesses across the three items, explains their differing methodological effects and proposes revisions suited to the research objective and intended respondents. Justifications should explain why the chosen changes address the identified problems. The learner should recognise that alternative wording and response formats may be appropriate under different research priorities and have a meaningful opportunity to improve selected aspects of the response after feedback.

commissions.title: Review and coherently redesign a questionnaire extract
commissions.specification_text:
Create a substantial but bounded Practice experience for university researchers involving independent questionnaire review, justified redesign, explanatory feedback and substantive improvement. The educational job is to develop independent, integrated and context-sensitive methodological judgement by extending the evaluative capability exercised in the preceding experiences to a coherent questionnaire extract. The learner should prioritise consequential problems, recognise relationships between design decisions and justify coherent improvements while considering credible alternatives. This remains formative Practice rather than a summative assessment, comprehensive questionnaire development project or specialist research methodology exercise.

RESEARCH CONTEXT AND QUESTIONNAIRE EVIDENCE
Use a realistic but explicitly fictional research scenario concerning university students' participation in extracurricular activities and their sense of belonging at university. The research objective is to investigate the relationship between recent participation in organised extracurricular activities and students' current sense of belonging, while identifying barriers that may limit participation. The intended respondents are currently enrolled students, including participants and non-participants. Define organised extracurricular activities as organised student clubs, societies, sports groups, volunteering opportunities and comparable activities outside formal course requirements. The researcher intends to examine associations between participation and belonging, not establish whether participation causes changes in belonging.

Present the following coherent draft questionnaire extract. Make clear that it has been constructed for learning purposes, is not taken from an actual survey and is not a validated research instrument.

Item 1: 'How often have you participated in extracurricular activities since starting university?' Response options: Never; Occasionally; Regularly; Very frequently.

Item 2: 'How many organised extracurricular activities have you attended in the past four weeks?' Response options: 0; 1–2; 2–4; 4 or more.

Item 3: 'Taking part in extracurricular activities has helped me make friends and feel that I belong at university.' Response options: Strongly disagree; Disagree; Neither agree nor disagree; Agree; Strongly agree.

Item 4: 'I feel that I belong at this university.' Response options: Strongly disagree; Disagree; Neither agree nor disagree; Agree; Strongly agree.

Item 5: 'Why have you not taken advantage of the many extracurricular opportunities available to you?' Select one response: Too busy; Too expensive; Not interested; Other.

Item 6: 'How satisfied are you with the accessibility and quality of extracurricular activities at your university?' Response options: Very dissatisfied; Dissatisfied; Neither satisfied nor dissatisfied; Satisfied; Very satisfied.

The draft contains no routing instructions or non-applicable response options. Preserve this feature because evaluating the suitability of questions for participants and non-participants is part of the intended methodological challenge. Item 4 provides a comparatively defensible design decision that need not automatically be revised. Do not identify it as such before the learner attempts the review.

The extract constitutes new first-pass unfamiliar evidence. Its subject matter, questionnaire formats and underlying evaluative principles remain comparable to those encountered in the preceding experiences. Assume general familiarity with questionnaires, research objectives and common response formats, but do not require specialist psychometric knowledge, statistical analysis or familiarity with a particular disciplinary research tradition. The earlier experiences have exercised the relationship between design weaknesses, methodological consequences and justified revisions. Reactivate this approach through the review brief without repeating introductory teaching or requiring access to earlier learner responses.

INDEPENDENT PRACTICE
Ask the learner to act as a researcher reviewing the draft questionnaire before it is distributed. Provide an overarching review brief requiring them to examine the complete extract against the stated research objective and intended respondent population, identify and prioritise consequential design weaknesses, explain their likely methodological effects and propose a coherent set of justified improvements.

Require attention to relationships between items where those relationships materially affect the usefulness of the resulting evidence. Ask learners to consider at least one meaningful alternative design decision or trade-off and justify their preferred approach. Allow learners to organise the review according to their own judgement rather than prescribe an item-by-item diagnostic sequence.

To protect the workload, require inspection of the complete extract but concentrate detailed written evaluation and revision on approximately three or four consequential problems or groups of related problems. A manageable expected performance comprises a brief statement of review priorities, selected substantive diagnoses, associated methodological explanations, revised questions or response formats and reasoned justifications. Related weaknesses may be addressed together. Learners may identify items that are sufficiently suitable to retain and explain their judgement where relevant. They may also recommend removing items whose contribution does not justify their inclusion. Do not require exhaustive line-by-line criticism, a fully rewritten questionnaire or detailed treatment of every minor imperfection.

The intended intellectual demand includes consideration of whether participation and belonging are being measured as distinguishable constructs, whether participation measures are comparable and interpretable, whether non-participants can respond meaningfully and whether proposed improvements introduce unnecessary respondent burden. These are commissioning-level design intentions, not a learner-facing diagnostic checklist. Do not reveal them as a list of problems to locate before the independent attempt. Frame learner-facing success expectations in general terms: relevance to the research objective, prioritisation of consequential issues, plausibility of methodological explanations, suitability of proposed improvements and quality of design justification.

EXPLANATORY FEEDBACK
After the learner has attempted the independent review, provide a concise but substantive reasoned evaluation of the actual questionnaire extract. Organise feedback around relationships between design decisions and the research objective rather than present an undifferentiated catalogue of questionnaire design rules. Distinguish consequential methodological problems from less important wording preferences. Illustrate credible improvements and alternatives without presenting a single complete model questionnaire as the uniquely correct solution.

Participation measurement and comparability: Items 1 and 2 potentially measure overlapping aspects of participation but use different reference periods and imprecise response formats. Item 1 may reflect cumulative experience and length of enrolment rather than recent participation. Its subjective frequency categories also limit comparability between respondents. Item 2 is more closely aligned with the objective of measuring recent participation, but its response categories overlap at two and four. It is also unclear whether respondents should count distinct activities or occasions of attendance. Explain how these weaknesses could make participation responses difficult to interpret or compare. Illustrate a revision such as: 'On how many occasions have you taken part in organised extracurricular activities in the past four weeks?' Response options: 0; 1–2; 3–4; 5–7; 8 or more. Explain that specifying attendance occasions and providing non-overlapping categories improves interpretability. Discuss the alternative of asking for the number of distinct activities if breadth of participation is the intended construct. Explain when retaining both recent and longer-term measures might be justified and when removing Item 1 would reduce unnecessary duplication. Recognise that the suitability of a four-week reference period may depend on academic calendar effects and the researcher's intended interpretation of recent participation.

Construct separation and interpretation: Item 3 combines friendship and belonging, which respondents may experience differently. It also asks respondents to attribute these experiences to extracurricular participation. Non-participants cannot necessarily answer meaningfully, and the item does not provide an independent measure of belonging. Explain why this matters when the research objective concerns the relationship between participation and belonging rather than respondents' perceptions of the benefits of participation. A response to Item 3 could conflate participation, perceived causal influence, friendship and belonging. Illustrate a defensible approach in which recent participation and current belonging are measured separately. If perceived benefits are relevant to an additional research objective, questions about those benefits could be separated into distinct constructs and directed only to respondents with relevant experience. Explain that separating constructs improves interpretability but does not by itself establish causation.

Retaining a defensible item: Item 4 provides a direct measure of self-reported belonging that does not require respondents to have participated in extracurricular activities. Its wording and balanced response scale are reasonably suitable for the bounded research objective. Explain why retaining an item can be a stronger methodological decision than revising it unnecessarily. Acknowledge that a single item may not capture every dimension of belonging and that a broader or validated instrument could be appropriate in a more extensive research design. Do not require learners to develop or validate such an instrument within this experience.

Barriers and respondent inclusion: Item 5 assumes respondents have not taken advantage of available opportunities and uses wording that may communicate criticism or a preferred behaviour. Its single-response format and restricted categories may not represent multiple barriers, students who experience no barriers or students who participate as much as they wish. Illustrate neutral wording such as: 'Which, if any, of the following factors limit your participation in organised extracurricular activities?' A suitable multiple-response format could include time commitments, cost, inconvenient scheduling, accessibility difficulties, lack of information, activities not matching interests, other factors and no factors limiting participation. Specify that the no-factors option is exclusive of substantive barriers. Explain that multiple selection can identify coexisting barriers, whereas a principal-barrier question may be preferable when the analytical purpose is to identify the most important obstacle. Distinguish lack of interest or preference not to participate from barriers that prevent desired participation where that distinction matters to the research objective. Discuss when routing is appropriate, recognising that existing participants may also experience barriers and should not automatically be excluded from relevant questions.

Construct coverage and questionnaire burden: Item 6 combines accessibility and quality, which respondents may evaluate differently. It may also require judgements that non-participants cannot reasonably make. Explain how a single satisfaction response could obscure whether dissatisfaction concerns access, quality or both. Consider whether the item contributes sufficiently to the stated research objective. A defensible redesign might remove it because the barriers question already addresses relevant accessibility concerns. Alternatively, if accessibility or quality is an important additional construct, the researcher could use separate, appropriately targeted questions with suitable eligibility or non-applicable options. Explain that removing an item can be a defensible improvement when its contribution to the intended evidence does not justify the additional demands on respondents.

Across the feedback, explain the methodological relationships between participation measures, belonging measures, barriers and the intended respondent population. Recognise that alternative revisions may be defensible depending on construct definitions, the intended analysis and the acceptable level of respondent effort. Discuss meaningful trade-offs involving measurement precision, construct coverage, response burden and analytical usefulness. Do not imply that the illustrative revisions are empirically validated or that a single questionnaire design is universally preferable. Keep the feedback sufficiently concise and organised for purposeful engagement within the allocated workload.

SUBSTANTIVE IMPROVEMENT
Invite the learner to revisit the existing questionnaire review after engaging with explanatory feedback. Ask them to improve selected aspects of their work where the feedback reveals a more consequential problem, a stronger design solution, an overlooked relationship between items or a more defensible methodological rationale. Encourage reconsideration of priorities as well as question wording.

A meaningful refinement could involve reconciling inconsistent participation measures, separating constructs, improving response options, reconsidering the treatment of non-participants, removing an unnecessary item or explaining why a preferred revision is more appropriate than an alternative. Where the learner's original decisions remain defensible, encourage greater precision in their justification or acknowledgement of a relevant limitation rather than require conformity to the illustrative feedback. Integrate the improvement into the existing written review and proposed revisions. Do not require a separate reflective essay, a comprehensive second review or a fully rewritten questionnaire.

WORKLOAD AND SCAFFOLDING
The authoritative allocation is thirty minutes of complete learner effort. Internally design for approximately four minutes of contextual reading, activation of familiar evaluative principles and first-pass inspection of the complete questionnaire extract; sixteen minutes of independent evaluation, prioritisation, revision and response construction; five minutes of explanatory feedback engagement; and five minutes of substantive refinement. Protect the independent reasoning and improvement time by limiting detailed written treatment to approximately three or four consequential problems or groups of related problems. Permit concise, structured review responses. Keep the scenario and questionnaire extract short, and organise feedback so that learners can engage purposefully with the most relevant methodological explanations. Use general review expectations rather than extensive procedural scaffolding. Increased challenge must arise from relationships between design considerations, the need to prioritise and the depth of methodological justification, not from unfamiliar disciplinary knowledge or unnecessarily extensive writing. No real survey data, external research, specialist software, tutor participation or empirical validation is required. Keep internal timing allocations out of learner-facing prose and do not frame completion speed as a performance criterion.

LEARNER EVIDENCE AND JOURNAL CONTRACT
Declare elicitation_id E3 for the learner's coherent written questionnaire review, including prioritised diagnoses, methodological explanations, proposed revisions, design justifications and consideration of alternatives. Retain the complete performance as one coherent learner-authored artefact. The elicitation must allow substantive improvement of the same response after feedback. Make its current content available through the journey-level Learning Journal as comm_3.E3. Do not require additional journal writing, comparison with earlier learner responses or reproduction of previous evaluations. Do not assume that a separate pre-feedback response is retained.

SUCCESS EXPECTATIONS
A defensible review identifies and prioritises consequential design weaknesses in relation to the research objective and intended respondents, explains their plausible methodological effects and proposes coherent improvements supported by reasoned justification. It recognises relevant relationships between questionnaire items, distinguishes important problems from acceptable design decisions and considers at least one meaningful alternative or trade-off. The learner has a substantive opportunity to strengthen the review or redesign through explanatory feedback. Success is not defined by reproducing a model questionnaire, identifying every possible weakness or rewriting every item. The resulting performance demonstrates bounded practice in integrated questionnaire evaluation and methodological judgement, not empirical validation of the proposed instrument.
